claim: A GoogLeNet trained on PlantVillage (54,306 lab images, 38 classes, 14 crops) reaches 99.35% on held-out PlantVillage but only about 31% on small verified sets of internet images taken in other conditions.
evidence: "accuracy of 99.35% on a held-out test set"; "overall accuracy of 31.40% in dataset 1, and 31.69% in dataset 2" (121 and 119 images)
plain: A model that scores almost perfectly on clean lab photos gets only about 1 in 3 right on real-world photos.
project_use: Reuse this as the main motivating number. Report in-domain and field accuracy separately and never treat PlantVillage test accuracy as evidence the model works in the field.

claim: In the PlantDoc paper, CNNs trained only on PlantVillage reach 15-40% accuracy on PlantDoc field images. Pretraining on PlantVillage and then fine-tuning on PlantDoc field data raises this to 60-70% on cropped leaves.
evidence: VGG16 PVD->PlantDoc uncropped 15.08%; PVD->cropped PlantDoc: VGG16 19.73%, InceptionV3 30.78%, InceptionResNetV2 39.87%; ImageNet+PVD then fine-tuned on C-PD: 60.41 / 62.06 / 70.53%
plain: Lab-trained models mostly fail on field photos, but showing them some labelled field photos roughly doubles their accuracy.
project_use: This is the natural baseline for our label-budget curve. Start from a PlantVillage-pretrained model, add k expert-labelled PlantDoc images per class, and track accuracy and selective-prediction metrics as k grows.

claim: PlantDoc is a small, publicly downloadable (CC-BY-4.0, GitHub) field dataset of 2,598 images over 13 species. Its class names were taken from PlantVillage's 38 classes, so most classes have a direct lab counterpart.
evidence: "2,598 data points in total across 13 plant species and up to 17 classes of diseases"; images collected "by using scientific and common names of 38 classes mentioned in the dataset by Mohanty et al."; train folders include Apple Scab/rust, Corn Gray leaf spot/leaf blight/rust, Potato early/late blight, Tomato (Early blight, Septoria, bacterial spot, late blight, mosaic virus, yellow virus, mold, spider mites), grape leaf black rot, plus healthy classes
plain: There is a free set of real-field leaf photos whose disease names mostly match the lab dataset, so we can train on lab photos and test on field photos with the same labels.
project_use: Use PlantVillage as the source and PlantDoc as the target, restricted to the overlapping classes for tomato, potato, apple, corn and grape. PlantDoc is small, so expert-label budgets must be counted in tens per class.

claim: PlantDoc has known label-noise and class-confusion problems: its authors admit some images may be mislabelled, and tomato bacterial spot and Septoria are hard to tell apart visually.
evidence: authors state "there are some images in the dataset which can potentially be wrongly classified"; Tomato Bacterial leaf spot and Septoria "looks similar and are hard to label using visual features alone"
plain: Some answers in the field test set may themselves be wrong, and some diseases look nearly identical even to people.
project_use: Treat PlantDoc labels as noisy. Report results for confusable class pairs and check whether 'I'm not sure' abstentions cluster on visually ambiguous classes, which is where expert review adds most value.

claim: The 2026 AgriPath-LF16 benchmark (111,307 images, 16 crops, 65 crop-disease pairs) shows that lab-only training collapses on field data: ResNet-50 macro-F1 falls from 96.7 to 4.3 and ConvNeXt-Tiny from 97.5 to 6.3. Even with mixed training, field F1 trails lab F1 by roughly 20-25% relative.
evidence: Lab-only: ResNet-50 96.7 lab -> 4.3 field; ConvNeXt-Tiny 97.5 -> 6.3; full training ResNet-50 97.2 lab vs 69.9 field; average relative lab-to-field drop ~25.6% CNNs, ~20.2% generative VLMs
plain: A recent large benchmark confirms that models trained only on lab photos almost completely fail in the field, and even models that saw some field photos still do much worse on them.
project_use: Gives an up-to-date number for the size of the shift. Its CNN vs CLIP/VLM comparison suggests a CLIP-style backbone is a reasonable second model if time allows.

claim: Other in-the-wild datasets exist, but some lack downloadable labels or cover only one crop. PlantWild has 18,542 images in 89 classes (56 diseased, 33 healthy) with a release promised via its project page. Plant Pathology 2020 has 3,651 expert-annotated apple images (scab, cedar apple rust, healthy). Plant Pathology 2021 grew to more than 23,000 images, includes multi-disease leaves, and adds two more disease categories.
evidence: PlantWild: "18,542 plant images", 89 classes, project page tqwei05.github.io/PlantWild; PP2020: "manually captured 3,651 high-quality, real-life symptom images", CNN "97% accuracy on a held-out test set"; PP2021: "from 3,651 last year to more than 23,000", task to "identify individual disease from multiple disease symptoms on a single leaf image"
plain: There are a few other real-world plant disease photo collections, but each has a catch: some are hard to get, some are apple-only, and some have several diseases on one leaf.
project_use: Keep PlantDoc as the main target. Plant Pathology (apple, overlaps PlantVillage apple scab and rust) could serve as a second shift test. Its multi-disease leaves are natural 'should abstain' cases, since a single-label classifier cannot be correct on them.

claim: Recent lab-to-field papers attribute the drop to shortcut learning on PlantVillage's uniform backgrounds but rarely measure calibration. AgriPath reports no ECE and only anecdotal evidence of confident wrong predictions.
evidence: TinyCNN (arXiv 2609.20290) Grad-CAM shows "off-leaf, background-driven attention consistent with shortcut learning"; AgriPath reports no calibration metrics, with qualitative cases of a CNN putting ~66% on the wrong class vs CLIP splitting late/early blight 45%/42%
plain: Lab-trained models seem to learn the plain lab background instead of the disease, and few studies check whether the model knows when it is wrong.
project_use: Measuring calibration (ECE, risk-coverage curves) on PlantDoc for a PlantVillage-trained model fills a real gap and is feasible in two weeks. Consider leaf cropping or background augmentation as a cheap shift mitigation.
